content.text:
This PostgreSQL 15 SELECT takes 20 seconds on a large table. How would you speed it up?

```sql
SELECT customer_id, MAX(created_at)
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
GROUP BY customer_id;
```

payload.last_agent_message:
I’d start by measuring the plan, then test a partial index containing only paid orders:

```sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT customer_id, MAX(created_at)
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
GROUP BY customer_id;
```

The plan will show whether the time goes into reading rows, sorting or aggregating, and whether those operations spill to disk. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` runs the query, so expect it to take roughly as long as the query itself. [PostgreSQL EXPLAIN documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/15/sql-explain.html)

A useful index to benchmark is:

```sql
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_paid_customer_created_idx
ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC NULLS LAST)
WHERE status = 'paid';
```

It keeps the index limited to paid rows, orders them by customer, and contains both values needed by the query. PostgreSQL may use an index-only scan and aggregate the ordered entries. Its benefit depends on how many orders are paid, the table’s visibility map, and the existing plan; a parallel sequential scan may still be faster when most rows qualify. Check `Heap Fetches` in the new plan, since recently modified pages can require table visits even in an index-only scan. [Partial indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/15/indexes-partial.html), [index-only scans](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/15/indexes-index-only-scans.html)

`CONCURRENTLY` permits writes during the build, but takes more work than a normal build and cannot run inside a transaction block. The index also costs storage and adds write overhead. [CREATE INDEX documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/15/sql-createindex.html)

**The key limit:** PostgreSQL 15 will generally still inspect all qualifying index entries for this grouped query; the index does not automatically jump to the latest order for each customer. If each customer has many paid orders, a bigger improvement may come from maintaining a summary table, or from probing the index once per customer using `LATERAL`—provided you already have a complete customer list and preserve the original query’s null semantics.

I’d compare plans before and after the index, check that statistics and autovacuum are current, and inspect any sort or hash spills before changing memory settings. The plan, paid-row fraction, and approximate number of customers would make it possible to recommend the best approach more confidently.
